extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, historians, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging historical writing and related literary criticism, emphasizing style, research, philosophical unity, and moral posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scepticism to events
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of scepticism, when it is not confined to events alone, but extends its doubts to all the principles of morality and religion, is by no means becoming in a great national historian, and will ... diminish the influence which the native genius of this singular man might well have entitled him to maintain over the minds of his countrymen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sceptical doubt may be useful in investigating facts, but a historian should not extend scepticism so far as to undermine moral or religious principles; such extension weakens the historian's authority and lasting influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer principle and feeling over sterile neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrow principles and views of things not perfectly just, are ... much better fitted for a great historian than no principles at all, and a deadening want of feeling, warmth, and passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians who hold (even imperfect) guiding principles and exhibit warmth and passion create interest and moral perspective; utter neutrality and emotional deadness produce lifeless history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not create interest merely by opposition or paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: When [principles and feeling] are removed, the only remaining means of creating interest in a historical work is the love of opposing the ruling opinions and of paradoxy. The leaning to this species of opposition is most evident in Hume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making contrarianism or paradox the sole engine of engagement; it is a weak substitute for genuine judgment, research, and sympathetic insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partisan predilection
rubrics_metrics.description: It is evident, that had he [Hume] written without any such views, he might have attained to an eminence far beyond that which he has reached, and descended to posterity not as the first of all party writers of history...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A historian should avoid letting party allegiance (political bias, preferring a dynasty or party) dictate interpretation; partisan slant reduces universal esteem and historical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough research and substance (import)
rubrics_metrics.description: In regard to style, few writers of any country can sustain a comparison with Robertson; his expressions are select and elegant... but he is very inferior in respect to other matters of far greater importance, — the research and import of his histories. The English themselves are now pretty well convinced that he is a careless, superficial, and blundering historian...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth of investigation, careful sourcing, and substantive import matter more than ornamental prose. Superficial research undermines credibility regardless of stylistic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple, clear, and careful style
rubrics_metrics.description: If we make this our object, the best style which we can adopt is the most simple; we should write clearly and carefully, but avoid all appearance of artifice, superfluity, affectation, or ambitiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is scientific or rigorous history, prioritize simplicity and clarity; avoid showy devices, unnecessary ornament, and pretension in diction and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbosity, antithesis, and oratorical affectations
rubrics_metrics.description: I think Robertson, although upon the whole a beautiful writer, is too fond both of verbosity and of antithesis. The ambition of fine writing, and of the desire to treat matters in an elaborate and oratorical manner, appear to me to be extremely erroneous and out of place in a writer of history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oratorical excesses (longwindedness, rhetorical antitheses) are inappropriate in historical writing and detract from the work's seriousness and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select, elegant, and unlaboured expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: In regard to style, few writers of any country can sustain a comparison with Robertson; his expressions are select and elegant, but always clear and unlaboured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for refined diction that nonetheless reads naturally and effortlessly; elegance should not come at the cost of clarity or seem laboured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive foreign/half‑Latin manner
rubrics_metrics.description: His [Gibbon's] style is full of Latin and French words and phrases. The English language ... has no very exact standard to regulate the proportion of the different elements ... That elaborate and half‑Latin manner of writing by which Gibbon is distinguished ... the English have now departed from it, and speak of it as a false species, and hostile to the spirit of their language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive use of foreign or Latinate constructions can seem affected and at odds with the native language; balance lexical influences to preserve idiomatic clarity and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate feeling, warmth, and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Gibbon is a writer full of thought: his language is in general powerful and exquisite, but it has, to a great excess, the faults of elaborateness, pompousness, and monotony. ... The work of Gibbon, however instructive and fascinating it may be, is nevertheless at bottom an offensive one, on account of his deficiency in feeling...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when intellectually rich, historical prose should convey human feeling and moral engagement; deficiency of feeling makes work less persuasive and less humane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite history and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: In every situation history and philosophy should be as much as possible united. Philosophy, if altogether separated from history, and destitute of the spirit of criticism...can become nothing more than a wild existence of sect and formality. History, on the other hand, without the animating spirit of philosophy, is merely a dead heap of useless materials, devoid of internal unity, proper purpose, or worthy result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical writing should incorporate philosophical perspective (a principled framework and critical reflection) so that facts cohere into meaning; neither pure narrative nor pure abstract philosophy alone suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide internal unity, purpose, and worthy result
rubrics_metrics.description: History...without the animating spirit of philosophy, is merely a dead heap of useless materials, devoid of internal unity, proper purpose, or worthy result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the work has an organizing idea or thesis that gives the collected facts direction and culminates in a meaningful conclusion or insight about human affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address essential human questions (origins, state, condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: How little is gained by all this as to the only real question, an answer to which should form the proper history of mankind! How little do we learn as to the origin and proper state, or the present lamentable and fallen condition of human nature!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad histories should aim to confront fundamental questions about human nature and destiny rather than merely aggregating ethnographic or travel details; seek explanatory depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of modern opportunities and instruments of information
rubrics_metrics.description: We have it in our power, however, to surpass [the ancients] in another way, namely, by considering history in a more scientific manner, and making use of those opportunities and instruments of information in which our times are so much superior to those of Greece and Rome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit archives, travel reports, documents, and other contemporary resources to produce more scientific, evidence‑based historical narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid materialistic/atomistic explanations of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all the foolish hypotheses which have ever cheated the human intellect with the empty show of explanation, that of materialism is the most unsatisfactory... in regard to morality, national welfare, and religion, its influences are utterly unworthy and pernicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about reductive, purely materialistic frameworks that deny spiritual, moral, or teleological dimensions; such frameworks may be intellectually unsatisfying and morally harmful in historical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground moral interpretation in reason or faith (a stable moral principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must have, in addition to [common sense and moral feeling], an eternal law of rectitude, derived not from experience and feeling, but from reason or from God. A fair and unshaken faith is indispensable for our welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that historical-moral judgments require a stable foundation (rational or religious) rather than relying solely on fluctuating feelings or common sense; historians should be explicit about their ethical foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing revelation and reason or over‑rationalizing religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Bonald errs by making Christianity too rational, and almost resolving it into reason. ... Many champions of Christianity have injured themselves by their too indiscriminating rejection of all philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When historians or philosophers integrate religious themes into history, avoid collapsing revelation entirely into rationalism or rejecting philosophical reasoning outright; maintain disciplined distinction and balance.
